export_users.description: Generate people and get the service's own CSV, JSON, XML or YAML rendering of them as a file you can download, attach to an email or hand to an import tool. This is the one action that returns the service's own field names rather than the tidied ones the other actions use, because an export is meant to be read by something else, and the one that hands back a file rather than data: 5,000 people is several megabytes, so the file is stored and only its opening lines come back inline. A seed is chosen for you when you do not give one, and reported, so any export can be produced again. No API key required.
export_users.name: export_users

parameters.description: How many people to put in the file, from 1 to 5,000.
parameters.name: count

parameters.description: How to render the people. CSV is one row each and opens in a spreadsheet, but it is the only format that drops the seed from the file, which is why a seed is always chosen and reported separately. Whichever you pick, the result is a file to download rather than text in the step.
parameters.name: export_format

options.label: CSV: one row per person, for a spreadsheet

parameters.description: Whether to draw only women, only men, or whichever comes up. This cannot be combined with a seed: the service silently ignores the gender whenever a seed is set, so asking for both fails the step rather than quietly returning a mix.
parameters.name: gender

parameters.description: Which countries the people should come from. Choose several and each person is drawn from one of them. Leave empty for all twenty-one. This decides the names, the address format, the phone numbers and the national ID number, but not the portraits, which are the same set for every country. Run 'List nationalities' to see what each one yields.
parameters.name: nationalities

options.label: NZ: New Zealand (no national ID number)

parameters.description: Any text. The same seed returns the same people every time, which is what makes a test fixture worth having. Leave empty and the service picks one and reports it back, so a run can be repeated afterwards. Avoid a seed of exactly 18 characters: that length has a special meaning to the service and is refused here.
parameters.name: seed

parameters.description: Which draw of the seed to take. Page 2 of a seed is a different set of people from page 1, not the next slice of one long list, so pages can overlap and cannot be stitched together into a bigger set. Use it to get more people from the same seed without changing the seed.
parameters.name: page

parameters.description: Which parts of a person to return. Leave empty for all of them. Narrowing this is worth doing for a large batch: the login hashes are the expensive part to generate. The nationality always comes back, whatever is chosen here. Use this or 'Leave out these fields', not both.
parameters.name: include_fields

options.label: Login: username, password, UUID and hashes

parameters.description: Which parts of a person to drop. Leave empty to keep everything. Handy for trimming a batch down to what a fixture actually needs. Use this or 'Only these fields', not both.
parameters.name: exclude_fields

generate_addresses.description: Generate invented postal addresses: street, city, state, postcode, country, latitude and longitude, and a time zone. Each address is written the way its country writes one, and comes with a ready-made single-line version for a label or an email. Use it to test an address form, a shipping calculator or a map pin. The coordinates are random rather than anywhere near the address, so treat them as two separate test values. No API key required.

generate_logins.description: Generate sign-in credentials for testing: a username, a password, the MD5, SHA-1 and SHA-256 hashes of that password with its salt, a UUID, and the name and email address they belong to. Choose which characters the passwords use and how long they run, or leave that empty to get real, commonly used passwords instead, which is the better fixture for testing a strength check. generate_names.description: Generate a list of invented people's names and nothing else: title, first name, last name, gender and nationality. Names are drawn from real name lists for each country, so a French batch reads French and a Serbian one reads Serbian. This is the fastest of the actions here because the service skips generating everything else. Use it for filling a leaderboard mockup, naming test accounts, or checking that a form copes with names outside your own alphabet. No API key required.

list_nationalities.description: List the twenty-one countries this integration can generate people from, with what each one yields: the national ID number it issues, or that it issues none, and what its postcodes look like. Worth reading before building a fixture on the assumption that everyone has an ID number: Iran, New Zealand, Turkey and Ukraine have none. This answers from what the pinned version of the service carries, so it costs no request and always works. No API key required.

nationalities.postcode_format: a UK-style postcode, such as EC1A 1BB

list_nationalities.name: list_nationalities

description: Generate invented people for testing, from a service that has been handing them out free since 2013. A person comes with a name, a gender, an email address, a postal address with coordinates and a time zone, phone and mobile numbers, a date of birth, a login with salted MD5, SHA-1 and SHA-256 hashes, a national ID number and a portrait photo. Ask for one or for five thousand, from any of twenty-one countries, and the names, addresses, phone numbers and ID numbers are written the way that country writes them. Give it a seed and the same people come back every time, which is what makes a test fixture worth keeping. Narrower actions return just names, just addresses, just logins or just passwords, and an export action hands back CSV, JSON, XML or YAML ready to write to a file. Nobody generated here is real and every email address is at example.com, which can never receive mail. Every action reads: nothing here changes anything, at the service or anywhere else. No account or API key required.
